summary.title: Effective learning: Twenty rules of formulating knowledge
summary.one_liner: You learn how to reformulate study material into short, simple, well-structured questions and answers so spaced repetition becomes faster and more durable.
keywords: how to memorize a long list
how to learn a poem by memory
why learn material you do not understand
takeaways: Do not memorize material you do not understand; build an overall picture first, then memorize details.
Keep each question and answer as short and simple as possible (minimum information principle), splitting complex items into several simpler ones.
Convert textbook sentences into cloze deletions, and convert sets into ordered enumerations or timeline-style questions.
Handle enumerations and poems with overlapping cloze deletions so that small chunks are practiced rather than the whole list at once.
Use images and graphic deletion (occlusion) where the visual benefit outweighs the cost of creating them; use mnemonics for only a small share of items.
summary.summary: This 1999 article by Piotr Wozniak, the creator of SuperMemo, gives twenty ordered rules for turning study material into items suited to spaced repetition. It explains each rule with worked before-and-after examples, such as rewriting a dense Dead Sea paragraph into short Q&A pairs and converting a list of EU members into a timeline of questions. The rules cover comprehension, building a basic picture before memorizing, cloze deletion, imagery and graphic deletion, mnemonics, and handling sets, enumerations and poems. It also includes SuperMemo-specific steps for creating cloze and occlusion items in several versions of the software.
